transcript:
Meeting header:
Date: 2025-10-16
Start: 14:30 PDT
Duration: 58 minutes
Attendees: Alex Chen (Redwood AE), Samira Patel (Redwood SE), Jordan Blake (Redwood SE), Priya Kaur (Saturn - Head of ML), Jorge Martinez (Saturn - Infra), Mei Lin (Saturn - Security), Ankit Rao (Saturn - SRE)
Recording note: call recorded via Zoom; auto-transcript present (medium quality)

Summary: technical deep-dive on prefix/prompt caching strategy for Saturn's multi-tenant chat product. Focus on hit rates, cache keys, tenant isolation, quantization compatibility, batching impacts, and VPC/on-prem constraints.

Transcript:
[00:00] Alex: Hey everyone, thanks for joining. quick intro \u0014 I'm Alex, AE on the account, Samira our SE who will lead the deep dive, and Jordan on solutions eng.
[00:18] Priya: Hi, thanks. we want to go pretty deep \u0014 our goals are to get token costs down and keep p95 latency under 220ms for interactive flows. we're also evaluating dedicated vs private deploy.
[00:30] Samira: great, that's the right tradeoff. we'll walk through the prefix caching model, typical hit rates by prompt shape, what keys look like, and how we prevent cross-tenant leakage.
[00:45] Jorge: quick infra context \u0014 we run a multi-tenant api gateway, and most inference is going to be on Dedicated but we may pilot Private VPC for sensitive customers. so network egress and KMS integration matter.
[01:05] Mei: security: SOC2 questions, audit logs, and we need assurance that cached prefixes can't expose another tenant's data.
[01:18] Samira: absolutely. on the last point we'll cover cache key construction and signing. there are a few patterns \u0014 raw prompt hashing, tenant scoping, and signed keys with a per-tenant secret.
[01:35] Jordan: can you start with a simple TTL/hit-rate example? what do you typically see for chat-like prompts?
[01:45] Samira: sure. typical conversational UX with system prompt + user few-shot examples \u0014 for a high-traffic prompt template, we often see 40-70% hot-prefix hit rates at the prefix level when users share the same system + initial user text. that's with a prefix defined as the first N tokens of model context. hit rate depends a lot on how many variables are templated vs free text.
[02:10] Priya: how are you defining prefix exactly \u0014 fixed token count or semantically (e.g., up to the first user turn)?
[02:20] Samira: both approaches exist. fixed-token prefixes (e.g., first 128 tokens) are simple and fast for the runtime to index. semantic boundaries (like up to the first user turn) can increase hit rate for conversational flows but require deterministic prompt canonicalization. tradeoffs: fixed-token is predictable; semantic needs robust parsing and may be brittle on slight variations.
[02:45] Jorge: and cache invalidation? if system prompt changes or a model version updates, what's the recommended approach?
[02:55] Samira: tag prefixes with model version and a config checksum. on model rollouts we atomically bump the prefix namespace so old hits automatically fall out. for system prompt changes include prompt hash in the key. TTLs are recommended \u0014 something like 24-72 hours for dynamic content, and longer for stable system prompts.
[03:20] Mei: what about multi-tenant safety \u0014 we can't have cross-tenant keys being served.
[03:28] Jordan: this is crucial. we namespace keys per-tenant and add HMAC signing using a tenant-specific secret. Redwood runtime supports per-tenant key namespaces and optional signed keys; then cache store is either per-tenant or shared with tenant id in key.
[03:45] Priya: are there perf implications for signing?
[03:50] Samira: signing is cheap \u0014 HMAC-SHA256 adds negligible CPU at request time; more important is where the cache lives. an in-memory local LRU on the GPU worker is fastest but ephemeral, while a shared Redis/KeyDB layer gives larger capacity but adds network hop. we tune local cache size + cold-miss prefetch to balance.
[04:12] Jorge: can you share numbers for latency improvements? e.g., p50/p95 improvements for a typical hit vs miss?
[04:20] Samira: on a hit we bypass most of the attention recompute; you see p50 drop by ~40-70% and p95 often drops by 30-60% depending on sequence length. absolute numbers: for our customers using Llama-like models, a prefix hit can drop token generation latency from ~120ms to ~40-60ms per chunk. that cascades to end-to-end interactive response time.
[04:52] Ankit: how does batching affect cache hits? we want high throughput batching on Dedicated pools.
[05:00] Samira: batching interacts with caching in two ways. first, cache-aware batching groups requests with identical cached prefixes to maximize reuse. second, large batch sizes increase throughput but can add latency for the slowest request in the batch. Redwood runtime supports dynamic batching windows that prioritize low-latency SLOs \u0014 you can set max batch size and max latency wait. For prefix caching, we tag requests with cache-key and the router will try to colocate compatible requests on the same worker.
[05:35] Priya: are there any consistency issues when using KV cache across workers?
[05:40] Jordan: if you rely on local KV cache on each worker, there's a higher miss rate than a shared Redis layer. Redwood offers an optional distributed KV layer with async propagation; we also support synchronous fetch-on-miss to the shared store. tradeoff: sync fetch increases per-request latency; async makes eventual consistent and may cause duplicate work. for critical low-latency flows we recommend local cache + warming/prewarm strategies.
[06:10] Mei: quantization \u0014 does changing precision break cache compatibility? e.g., run 4-bit quantized model vs 8-bit?
[06:18] Samira: great question. cache contents (KV cache) are model-architecture and quantization specific. you must only reuse a prefix cached from an identical model binary and quantization. that's why model-version + quantization profile must be included in the cache key. mixing quant levels will corrupt internal KV state.
[06:40] Priya: we do periodic quantization experiments \u0014 could we safely share prefixes across quant steps if we transcode?
[06:48] Jordan: no safe, general transcoding. converting KV states between quantization schemes is non-trivial and not recommended. best practice: treat each quantized model as separate cache namespace.
[07:00] Ankit: on Private VPC deployments, where does the cache live? within customer VPC?
[07:06] Samira: options: 1) local ephemeral cache in the inference pods (default in Dedicated/Private), 2) shared Redis inside the VPC (recommended for stateful large caches), or 3) Redwood-managed cache in a private peered setup (we only do this under strict contracts). For regulated CUs Saturn should run the shared Redis inside the same VPC \u0014 avoids egress and keeps data local.
[07:34] Mei: encryption and KMS \u0014 if we sign keys or store prefixes, do we need to encrypt cached values at rest?
[07:40] Jordan: we recommend encrypting shared cache at rest using customer-managed keys (KMS/HSM). Redwood supports encryption-at-rest for managed caches and integration with customer KMS for Private deployments. Also audit logs for cache access are available.
[07:58] Priya: what's the best approach to measuring hit rates in production?
[08:03] Samira: instrument the router to emit metrics at per-template level: cache_keys_requested, cache_hits, cache_miss_latency. Redwood Console can show per-route hit-rate, and you can tie this to sample prompts to understand when prefixes diverge. Start with a conservative prefix length and increase until hit-rate plateaus.
[08:25] Ankit: Do you recommend canonicalization of user-provided free text to improve hits?
[08:29] Samira: yes but carefully. simple normalization (whitespace, punctuation trimming, lowercasing for certain templates) improves hit-rate. but aggressive canonicalization can change semantics \u0014 e.g., punctuation in code blocks. So we recommend template-level rules and whitelist fields safe to normalize.
[08:50] Priya: any rules of thumb for prefix token length?
[08:54] Samira: depends on the model and prompt variability. 64 tokens for very templated system prompts, 128 tokens is a good default for mixed templates, 256+ if you have long fixed context. monitor hit-rate vs. memory cost curve. more prefix tokens increases cache size exponentially in some workloads.
[09:12] Jorge: eviction policies \u0014 LRU vs TTL vs LFU?
[09:17] Jordan: LRU is simple and works well for locality. LFU helps for long-tail stable prefixes. TTLs are important to ensure stale system prompts or model updates don't linger. A hybrid: LRU with per-key TTL and occasional compaction works well in practice.
[09:33] Mei: auditability \u0014 can we get per-tenant cache access logs?
[09:37] Samira: yes, audit logs include cache-get/cache-set events with tenant id and key hash. we avoid logging raw prompt text in logs for PII reasons; logs record key hashes and sample prompts can be routed to secure storage.
[09:55] Priya: curious about warm-start strategies for new workers after autoscale \u0014 cold miss problem drives latency spikes.
[10:02] Jordan: two approaches: 1) proactive prewarm \u0014 when a new worker starts, it fetches top-N hot prefixes from shared store; 2) background async prefetch based on recent access patterns. prewarm costs network but smooths tail latency. Redwood supports both strategies with configurable thresholds.
[10:24] Ankit: what about cost modeling \u0014 how much memory per prefix?
[10:28] Samira: depends on model hidden size and prefix token count. rough back-of-envelope: for a 7B model with 4096-hidden dims, each token's KV entry can be tens to low hundreds of bytes after quantization/packing. so 128-token prefix might be on the order of a few KB. you should run sample instrumentation on your own model configs; we can share a spreadsheet.
[10:52] Priya: let's discuss an example flow \u0014 our support chat template, system prompt + two user messages + metadata. how to configure keys?
[11:00] Samira: key schema we recommend: tenant_id | model_id | model_version | quant_profile | prompt_template_id | prefix_hash | optional_ttl. Include HMAC signature: HMAC(tenant_secret, key_components) to prevent spoofing. On the runtime side Redwood will validate signature and enforce tenant scoping.
[11:25] Mei: are there any security risks if tenant_secret leaks?
[11:30] Jordan: yes, if secret leaks someone could forge cache hits in shared caches. mitigate by rotating secrets quarterly, using KMS to manage secrets, and limiting shared cache access with network-level controls and RBAC. Recommend per-tenant secrets stored in KMS and not in plaintext on nodes.
[11:48] Priya: any gotchas for caching with tool/function calling or structured outputs?
[11:53] Samira: function-calling often depends on dynamic user data so hit rates can be lower. however, if the initial reasoning prefix is shared, caching helps. structured outputs where exact tokenization matters \u0014 ensure you canonicalize templates and treat variable inserts as separate fields not part of the cached prefix.
[12:15] Alex: quick note on benchmarking \u0014 we'll share a benchmark harness that replays your production logs and measures hit rates for different prefix lengths and canonicalization rules.
[12:25] Priya: that would be very helpful.
[12:28] Jorge: any recommendation for Redis sizing for shared cache?
[12:31] Samira: size for expected number of hot prefixes times average prefix size plus eviction headroom. also factor in replication, persistence options. we usually recommend a dedicated Redis cluster inside the VPC with at least 2x the estimated working set and replication for failover.
[12:50] Mei: compliance \u0014 does Redwood store raw prompts if using managed cache?
[12:55] Jordan: for managed cache we store key-hashes and encrypted values; raw prompts are not stored unless you opt-in for debugging. on Private deployments customer data remains in their VPC per contract.
[13:10] Priya: what's the recommended rollout path?
[13:13] Samira: start with read-through cache analytics in sandbox: instrument hit/miss, test prefix lengths, enable per-tenant namespaces and signed keys, then pilot on Dedicated with small percent traffic for 2 weeks, then expand. For high-security customers run pilot on Private VPC.
[13:30] Alex: ok let's summarize next steps and action items.
[13:35] Priya: thanks all, that was very practical.
